questions.prompt: One of the four readers of lesson 25 makes this remark: a woman who spends three hours on the telephone with her friends is called sociable, and the same woman, spending the same three hours writing to those same friends on the net, is called cut off from real life. Which word of the lesson names a judgement of that kind, one that rests on no reason at all?

options.text: obvious
irrational
preoccupied
aggressive

questions.explanation: "irrational" is the word: the two judgements praise and blame exactly the same three hours, so nothing supports the difference between them, and irrational is precisely what no reason supports. "obvious" says the contrary of what the remark shows: obvious means so clear that nobody needs to be told, whereas the whole point of the reader's remark is that the difference cannot be defended once you look at it. "preoccupied" describes a mind that cannot stop turning round one thing; it is a state of a person, not a judgement passed on somebody else. And "aggressive" describes a way of reacting, ready to attack in words or in acts; the two judgements here are unfair, which is a different fault altogether.

questions.prompt: The Wednesday session of a science club in El Kef used to be half empty at four o'clock. Last term pupils began queuing for a place at the benches, and last week ten of them had to be turned away. Complete the note in the club's log: "The Wednesday session is getting ___."

options.text: less and less crowded
much more crowded
more and more crowded
more crowded and crowded

questions.explanation: "more and more crowded" is right: half empty, then a queue, then ten pupils turned away is an increase that has not stopped, and English marks a change that goes on with two comparatives joined by and. "less and less crowded" is correctly built but points the wrong way: it would say the room is emptying, which is the opposite of the three facts given. "much more crowded" measures a difference at one moment and says nothing about a change that continues; it would fit a comparison between two rooms, not the story of one room over a term. And "more crowded and crowded" keeps only half of the structure. Crowded has two syllables and ends in -ed, so it builds its comparative with more and not with an ending, and it is that more which is doubled: more and more crowded. It is the short adjectives that repeat their whole -er form on each side of and, longer and longer, colder and colder. The two lines of the rule are separate, and neither one is a shortening of the other.

questions.prompt: On Monday afternoon, in the club's computer room, Hedi said to Rania: "I am moving the second printer here today." On Thursday, standing in that same room, Rania passes his words on to a friend who has just arrived. Which line does she say?

options.text: He said he was moving the second printer here that day.
He said he was moving the second printer there that day.
He said he was moving the second printer here today.
He said he was moving the second printer there today.

questions.explanation: "He said he was moving the second printer here that day." is the line, and it is the only one that asks the right question of each word instead of copying a table. Here points at the place of the person speaking: Rania is standing in the very room Hedi called here, so the word still points where it should and it stays. Today points at the day of the person speaking, and Rania is speaking three days later, so today would now name Thursday and not Monday; it has to become that day. The verb moves too, because said is a past, and am moving becomes was moving. "He said he was moving the second printer there that day." gets the day right and then sends the printer to some other room, although Rania and her friend are inside the one that was meant. "He said he was moving the second printer here today." keeps the room, rightly, and then promises the printer for Thursday, which is not what Hedi said. And "He said he was moving the second printer there today." gets both words wrong at once. The table of time and place words is a default, never a law: ask each time whether the word would still point at the right place and the right moment.

questions.prompt: A radio journalist is passing on to her listeners, live, what her guest is saying in the studio at that very moment. The guest: "I spend two hours a day on the club's website." The journalist begins: "Our guest says ___" How does she finish?

options.text: that he spent two hours a day on the club's website.
that he was spending two hours a day on the club's website.
that he had spent two hours a day on the club's website.
that he spends two hours a day on the club's website.

questions.explanation: "that he spends two hours a day on the club's website." is right: before touching any tense you look at the verb that introduces the report, and here it is says, a present. When the reporting verb is in the present, the present perfect or the future, no tense moves at all; only the pronoun does, and I becomes he. "that he spent two hours a day on the club's website." steps the verb back one tense, which is what you would do after said, not after says. "that he had spent two hours a day on the club's website." steps it back twice over and pushes into the past a habit the guest has at this moment. And "that he was spending two hours a day on the club's website." changes the tense and the aspect together, turning a habit into an action in progress, which is not what the guest said.

questions.prompt: A magazine prints a self-test of seven questions on time spent online and adds one line of its own: five yes answers or more, and it calls the reader an addict. A reader answers yes to four of the seven. What does the test itself allow you to conclude about him?

options.text: That he is an addict, because four out of seven is more than half.
Nothing: the test sets its own line at five, and he is below it.
That he is a milder addict than a reader who answers yes five times.
That he will become an addict as soon as he answers one more yes.

questions.explanation: "Nothing: the test sets its own line at five, and he is below it." is right: a rule with a threshold speaks only above that threshold, and says nothing whatever about the cases underneath it. Four is not five, and the honest reading stops there. "That he is an addict, because four out of seven is more than half." replaces the rule the document actually printed with an arithmetic of your own; the test never mentioned a half. "That he is a milder addict than a reader who answers yes five times." invents a degree the test does not have: it offers one line and two sides, not a scale. And "That he will become an addict as soon as he answers one more yes." turns a count of answers into a prediction about a person's future, which no questionnaire can make. Remember in any case what this document is: a magazine test, not a medical opinion.
